The Story of King Subhaum

I bow to Lord Jinendra, whose feet are worshipped by gods of all four types, and I write the story of the eighth Chakravartin, Subhaum.

Subhaum was the son of King Kartavirya of Irshyavan and Queen Revati. The Chakravartin had a cook named Jaysen. One day, when the Chakravartin sat down to eat, the cook served him hot-hot kheer. It burned the Chakravartin's mouth, and he became very angry with the cook. In his rage, he struck the cook on the head with the very hot vessel of kheer. The cook's entire head was burned. Dying in terrible agony, he was reborn as a Vyantar god in the Salt Ocean.

Through his clairvoyance, he knew the story of his past life, and his anger toward the Chakravartin knew no bounds. Revenge made his life restless. So he disguised himself as an ascetic, holding beautiful, fragrant fruits, and went to the Chakravartin. He offered the fruits as a gift. The Chakravartin ate them and was greatly pleased. He asked the ascetic, "Maharaj, these fruits are extraordinarily sweet. Where did you get them? And where can more be found?"

The Vyantar deceived him, saying, "In the middle of the ocean, there is a small island. That is my home. Please grace my home with your presence, and I shall offer you many more such excellent, sweet fruits. There are many gardens of such fruits there." The Chakravartin, caught by greed, fell for the Vyantar's trick and went with him. When they reached the middle of the ocean, the Vyantar revealed his true form and said in great anger, "Sinner, do you know why I brought you here? If not, listen — I was your cook Jaysen, and you burned me to death without mercy. Now I have brought you here to take revenge. Tell me, where will you go now? Prepare to suffer the fruit of what you did. This is the fate of sinners like you. But listen, there is still a way you can escape. If you write the Panch Namaskar Mantra in the water and erase it with your feet, I can let you go alive."

For the sake of saving his life, who would not do anything? He does not stop to consider whether it is good or bad. The Chakravartin, desperate to save his life, wrote the sacred mantra in the water and erased it with his feet — thus committing the grave sin of desecrating the holy mantra. Through this sin, he fell into hell after death, where he suffered for countless ages.

Eventually, through the ripening of residual merit, he regained human form. He remembered his past folly, took initiation as a monk, and through dedicated spiritual practice, ultimately attained liberation.

This story teaches two important lessons. First, that anger and violence toward others create karmic debts that must be repaid. The Chakravartin's cruel treatment of his cook led to his own destruction. Second, that even in desperation, one should never commit sin to save oneself. The Chakravartin's desecration of the sacred mantra compounded his suffering rather than relieving it. The wise should practise non-violence and never compromise their spiritual principles, even in the face of death.
